Groundwater depletion under recurrent drought: evidence from 42 aquifers

Authors

  • Chidi Okafor Department of Civil Engineering, University of Lagos
  • Anna Lindqvist Department of Earth Sciences, Uppsala University

DOI:

https://doi.org/10.5555/jhs.2024.0173

Abstract

Recurrent multi-year droughts are accelerating groundwater depletion worldwide, yet most assessments rely on single-event snapshots. We compiled monthly water-table records from 42 monitored aquifers on four continents between 1990 and 2022. Aquifers that experienced two or more drought episodes lost storage 2.6 times faster than those that experienced one, and recovery after rainfall returned was incomplete in 31 of the 42 systems.

1. Introduction

Groundwater supplies roughly half of the water used for irrigation worldwide and is the primary buffer against surface-water shortfalls during drought. When rainfall fails, pumping rises precisely when natural recharge falls, and the resulting decline in water tables can persist for decades after the drought itself has ended.

2. Data and methods

We used monitoring-well records with at least 25 years of monthly observations, harmonized to a common datum. Drought episodes were identified with the Standardized Precipitation Index at a 12-month scale, using a threshold of −1.5 sustained for at least six consecutive months.

3. Results

Median storage loss was 0.41 metres per year in aquifers with repeated droughts, against 0.16 metres per year in aquifers with a single episode. Recovery was incomplete in 31 of the 42 aquifers after the most recent drought.
